title: Sikhism: the free kitchen
hookLine: in every gurdwara, anyone may eat, sitting together on the floor as equals

lines: A LONG HALL, ROWS ON THE FLOOR.
NO NAMES, NO BILL, NO BETTER SEAT.
cards: A long hall, a clean floor, long strips of cloth laid down in rows. A student sits down. Next to her, a taxi driver still in his work jacket.

Then a grandmother, a tourist with a backpack, a man who hasn't eaten since yesterday. Volunteers walk the rows with buckets and ladles: lentils, a vegetable curry, warm flatbread dropped into open hands.
Nobody asks your name, your religion or whether you can pay. Nobody gets a better seat. This is the free kitchen, and the idea of sitting together.

teach.b: The word is langar: the community kitchen that belongs to every gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship, and also the meal served there. Sikh tradition traces it to Guru Nanak, the first Guru.

teach.h: GURU NANAK, GURU ANGAD, MATA KHIVI.
teach.b: It grew under the second Guru, Guru Angad, and Sikhs especially remember his wife, Mata Khivi, who ran the kitchen and made sure the food was generous. Sikh tradition remembers why it mattered.
In that world, who could eat with whom was bound up with caste, and eating side by side crossed lines people had been raised not to cross.
The third Guru, Guru Amar Das, made it a rule, remembered in a short Punjabi phrase: pehle pangat, piche sangat.
First sit in the row, then join the gathering. A story Sikhs tell says even the Mughal emperor Akbar, coming to see the Guru, first sat on the floor and ate in the row like everyone else.
The historical details of that visit are debated, but the point of the story isn't.
The food is simple and vegetarian, so people of almost any diet or faith can eat it. Volunteers cook and serve it as seva, selfless service.

And it runs at every scale, from a small gurdwara's kitchen to the vast langar at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where still nobody pays. So langar holds two lessons. Yesterday's: share what you have.
Today's: when you share, sit at the same level. Nobody above, nobody below.

how: Gurdwaras keep a langar where volunteers cook and serve a free vegetarian meal to anyone who comes, traditionally seated together in rows on the floor.

a special table is set for him.

practice: Picture a row on a floor, and put yourself in it. Fill the places beside you: someone you love, someone you pass every day and never speak to, someone you find hard, all at the same height, with the same plate.
Notice where that's easy and where it pinches.

wordCard.voice: Langar. The free community kitchen of the gurdwara, and the meal shared there, where everyone eats at the same level. Today's word.
